questions.q: To whom did Nebuchadnezzar send the decree?
questions.a: Nebuchadnezzar sent the decree to all peoples, nations, and languages who lived on the earth.

questions.q: Why did Nebuchadnezzar send the decree?
questions.a: Nebuchadnezzar sent the decree to tell everyone about the signs and wonders the Most High had done for him.

questions.q: What did Nebuchadnezzar say about the Most High?
questions.a: Nebuchadnezzar said that the Most High’s signs are great and his wonders are mighty, that his kingdom lasts forever, and that he rules over every generation.

questions.q: How was Nebuchadnezzar living before he had his dream?
questions.a: Nebuchadnezzar was living securely in his house and prospering in his palace.

questions.q: What made Nebuchadnezzar afraid?
questions.a: A dream that Nebuchadnezzar saw frightened him, and the thoughts and visions in his mind alarmed him.

questions.q: Why did Nebuchadnezzar issue a decree to bring before him all the wise men of Babylon?
questions.a: Nebuchadnezzar wanted the wise men of Babylon to come and interpret his dream for him.

questions.q: What happened when Nebuchadnezzar told his dream to the magicians, enchanters, Chaldeans, and diviners?
questions.a: They were not able to tell Nebuchadnezzar what the dream meant.

questions.q: What was Daniel’s Babylonian name and what was Daniel’s position in Nebuchadnezzar’s kingdom?
questions.a: Daniel’s Babylonian name was Belteshazzar and he held the position of “chief of the magicians.”

questions.q: Who did Nebuchadnezzar believe was able to tell the interpretation of his dream?
questions.a: Nebuchadnezzar believed Daniel could interpret his dream for him, for Nebuchadnezzar said of Daniel, “the spirit of the holy gods is in you, so no mystery is too hard for you to explain.”

questions.q: What did Nebuchadnezzar see in the first part of his dream?
questions.a: Nebuchadnezzar saw a great, strong, beautiful tree that reached to the heavens. It provided shade for animals and an abode for the birds. It had abundant fruit that fed all living creatures.

questions.q: What did the holy messenger from the heavens say to do to the tree?
questions.a: The holy messenger said to chop down the tree, cut off its branches, strip off its leaves and scatter its fruit.

questions.q: What was to be done with the tree stump?
questions.a: The stump was to be left in the earth, bound with a band of iron and bronze. Let it be wet with dew. Let it live with the animals. Let his mind be that of an animal and not of a man for seven years.

questions.q: What was the purpose of doing this to the tree in Nebuchadnezzar’s dream?
questions.a: The purpose was to show Nebuchadnezzer that those who are alive would know that the Most High rules over the kingdoms of peoples and gives them to anyone he wishes to place over them.

questions.q: What did Nebuchadnezzar tell Belteshazzar about his other wise men?
questions.a: Nebuchadnezzar said that none of his other wise men were able to tell him the interpretation of the dream, but Belteshazzar was able because the spirit of the holy gods was in him.

questions.q: How did Daniel react when he first understood the dream?
questions.a: Daniel was appalled for a moment, and his thoughts alarmed him.

questions.q: What details did Daniel repeat about the tree Nebuchadnezzar saw in his dream?
questions.a: Daniel said the tree had become great and strong, reached to the heavens, and could be seen from all the earth; it had beautiful leaves and much fruit, and animals and birds lived in it.

questions.q: Who did Daniel say the tree was in Nebuchadnezzar’s dream?
questions.a: Daniel said the tree was Nebuchadnezzar.

questions.q: What did Daniel say the holy messenger told Nebuchadnezzar to do to the tree?
questions.a: Daniel said the holy messenger told Nebuchadnezzar to cut down the tree but leave its stump bound with iron and bronze in the field, wet with dew, until seven times passed over him.

questions.q: Whose decree did Daniel say was coming upon King Nebuchadnezzar?
questions.a: Daniel said it was the decree of the Most High that was coming upon King Nebuchadnezzar.

questions.q: What was to happen to Nebuchadnezzar until he acknowledged that the Most High rules over the kingdoms of people and gives them to anyone he wishes?
questions.a: Nebuchadnezzar was to be driven from among men. He would live in the fields with the wild animals and eat grass like an ox and be wet with the dew from the heavens.

questions.q: How long was it to be before Nebuchadnezzar would acknowledge that the Most High rules over the kingdoms of people and he gives them to anyone he wishes?
questions.a: Seven years were to pass until Nebuchadnezzar acknowledged that the Most High rules over the kingdoms of people and he gives them to anyone he wishes.

questions.q: What did leaving the stump of the tree represent?
questions.a: Leaving the stump represented that Nebuchadnezzar’s kingdom would remain for him once he acknowledged that heaven rules.

questions.q: After interpreting the dream for Nebuchadnezzar, what was Daniel’s advice for him?
questions.a: Daniel advised Nebuchadnezzar to stop sinning and to do what was right. He also told Nebuchadnezzar to turn away from his sins by showing mercy to the poor.

questions.q: How long was it before the interpretation of Nebuchadnezzar’s dream began to happen?
questions.a: All these things began to happen twelve months after his dream.

questions.q: What did Nebuchadnezzar say about himself as he looked at Babylon?
questions.a: Nebuchadnezzar said that he had built Babylon by his own power and for the glory of his majesty.

questions.q: What happened while Nebuchadnezzar was still speaking?
questions.a: A voice from heaven said that the kingdom had passed from Nebuchadnezzar.

questions.q: What did the voice from heaven say would happen to Nebuchadnezzar?
questions.a: The voice said Nebuchadnezzar would be driven away from people to live with the wild animals and eat grass like an ox until he acknowledged that the Most High rules over the kingdoms of people.

questions.q: What happened to Nebuchadnezzar immediately after the voice spoke?
questions.a: Nebuchadnezzar was driven away from people, ate grass like oxen, and his hair grew long like eagles’ feathers and his nails like birds’ claws.

questions.q: What happened to Nebuchadnezzar at the end of the seven years?
questions.a: Nebuchadnezzar’s sanity was restored to him.

questions.q: What did Nebuchadnezzar do after his sanity was restored to him?
questions.a: Nebuchadnezzar praised and honored the Most High who rules forever.

questions.q: What did Nebuchadnezzar say about the Most High’s power over the earth and the heavens?
questions.a: Nebuchadnezzar said that the Most High regards all the people of earth as nothing and does as he wishes among the army of heaven and the people of earth, and no one can stop him or question what he does.

questions.q: What happened to Nebuchadnezzar’s kingdom?
questions.a: The kingdom was given back to him.

questions.q: What was Nebuchadnezzar’s final statement concerning the King of heaven?
questions.a: Nebuchadnezzar said, “Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and honor the King of heaven, for all his deeds are right and his ways are just. He is able to humble anyone who is proud.”

commentary.text: Nebuchadnezzar acknowledges the power of Jehovah. (Dan. 4:1-18) Daniel interprets his dream. (Dan. 4:19-27) The fulfilment of it. (Dan. 4:28-37)

Dan. 4:1-18 The beginning and end of this chapter lead us to hope, that Nebuchadnezzar was a monument of the power of Divine grace, and of the riches of Divine mercy. After he was recovered from his madness, he told to distant places, and wrote down for future ages, how God had justly humbled and graciously restored him. When a sinner comes to himself, he will promote the welfare of others, by making known the wondrous mercy of God. Nebuchadnezzar, before he related the Divine judgments upon him for his pride, told the warnings he had in a dream or vision. The meaning was explained to him. The person signified, was to be put down from honour, and to be deprived of the use of his reason seven years. This is surely the sorest of all temporal judgments. Whatever outward affliction God is pleased to lay upon us, we have cause to bear it patiently, and to be thankful that he continues the use of our reason, and the peace of our consciences. Yet if the Lord should see fit by such means to keep a sinner from multiplying crimes, or a believer from dishonouring his name, even the dreadful prevention would be far preferable to the evil conduct. God has determined it, as a righteous Judge, and the angels in heaven applaud. Not that the great God needs the counsel or concurrence of the angels, but it denotes the solemnity of this sentence. The demand is by the word of the holy ones, God's suffering people: when the oppressed cry to God, he will hear. Let us diligently seek blessings which can never be taken from us, and especially beware of pride and forgetfulness of God.

Dan. 4:19-27 Daniel was struck with amazement and terror at so heavy a judgment coming upon so great a prince, and gives advice with tenderness and respect. It is necessary, in repentance, that we not only cease to do evil, but learn to do good. Though it might not wholly prevent the judgment, yet the trouble may be longer before it comes, or shorter when it does come. And everlasting misery will be escaped by all who repent and turn to God.

Dan. 4:28-37 Pride and self-conceit are sins that beset great men. They are apt to take that glory to themselves which is due to God only. While the proud word was in the king's mouth, the powerful word came from God. His understanding and his memory were gone, and all the powers of the rational soul were broken. How careful we ought to be, not to do any thing which may provoke God to put us out of our senses! God resists the proud. Nebuchadnezzar would be more than a man, but God justly makes him less than a man. We may learn to believe concerning God, that the most high God lives for ever, and that his kingdom is like himself, everlasting, and universal. His power cannot be resisted. When men are brought to honour God, by confession of sin and acknowledging his sovereignty, then, and not till then, they may expect that God will honour them; not only restore them to the dignity they lost by the sin of the first Adam, but add excellent majesty to them, from the righteousness and grace of the Second Adam. Afflictions shall last no longer than till they have done the work for which they were sent. There can be no reasonable doubt that Nebuchadnezzar was a true penitent, and an accepted believer. It is thought that he did not live more than a year after his restoration. Thus the Lord knows how to abase those that walk in pride, but gives grace and consolation to the humble, broken-hearted sinner who calls upon Him.
